summary: Defines OSPFv2 Opaque LSAs using TLV structures to attach more attributes to prefixes or links. They are optional and backward compatible, and go beyond the fixed-format LSAs of RFC 2328.

eli5.summary: Maps in a routing protocol get a place to add sticky notes with extra details.

subtitle: Optional, TLV-based Opaque LSAs that let OSPFv2 attach extra attributes to prefixes and links.

tldr.problem: OSPFv2's fixed-format Link State Advertisements cannot easily carry new information, yet new needs such as source/destination routing, route tagging and segment routing call for more attributes on prefixes and links.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two Opaque LSAs, Extended Prefix (Opaque Type 7) and Extended Link (Opaque Type 8), built from Type-Length-Value tuples whose sub-TLVs can carry the extra attributes.
tldr.outcome: The new LSAs are optional and fully backward compatible, so routers that do not understand them keep working. The RFC itself defines only the framework and two top-level TLVs; applications define the actual attributes.

today: RFC 7684 is a Proposed Standard and no RFC obsoletes or updates it. It supplies the framework, and other specifications define the actual sub-TLVs.

sections.title: Why Extend OSPFv2
sections.content:
OSPFv2, described in RFC 2328, advertises routing information in fixed-format Link State Advertisements (LSAs). That format cannot readily be stretched to carry new kinds of information. The RFC names source/destination routing, route tagging and segment routing as new requirements that need such an extension.

The solution is a pair of Opaque LSAs built from Type-Length-Value (TLV) tuples. They attach additional attributes to prefixes or links, whether or not those prefixes and links are also advertised in the fixed-format LSAs. The Opaque LSAs are optional and fully backward compatible. The RFC contrasts this with OSPFv3, where existing LSAs are to be replaced by TLV-based extended LSAs.
sections.eli5: The old OSPF forms have no space for new details. So this RFC adds a flexible extra page that can hold any new notes.

sections.title: The TLV Format and Opaque IDs
sections.content:
The body of both new LSAs is a list of TLVs, in the same format used by the Traffic Engineering extensions to OSPFv2. Each TLV has a 16-bit Type, a 16-bit Length and a value. Length counts only the value, in octets, so a TLV with no value has a length of 0. TLVs nest, and nested TLVs are called sub-TLVs.

Every TLV is padded with zeros to 4-octet alignment, and padding is not counted in Length. A 3-octet value therefore has Length 3 but occupies 8 octets in total. The LSA's own Length field covers the LSA header and all TLVs, including padding.

The Opaque ID has no meaning except to tell apart several LSAs of the same kind from one router. If several LSAs carry the same prefix or link, the attributes from the one with the lowest Opaque ID are used.
sections.eli5: Each note has a label, a size and the content, and is padded so everything lines up neatly. If two notes say different things about the same road, the one with the lowest number wins.

sections.title: The Extended Prefix Opaque LSA
sections.content:
The OSPFv2 Extended Prefix Opaque LSA uses Opaque Type 7 and advertises extra attributes for prefixes carried in Router-LSAs, Network-LSAs, Summary-LSAs (IP network), NSSA-LSAs and AS-external-LSAs. A router can advertise several of them. The LS Type may be 10 (area-local flooding) or 11 (AS-wide flooding), and the advertising router controls the scope. Sometimes the flooding scope is wider than that of the prefixes, as in a segment routing mapping server deployment.

Its one top-level TLV is the Extended Prefix TLV (type 1). It holds a Route Type, a Prefix Length in bits, an address family (AF), a Flags octet, the Address Prefix and optional sub-TLVs. Because the LSA type fixes the flooding scope, the scope MUST satisfy the needs of every prefix in one LSA.

  • Route Type: 0 Unspecified, 1 Intra-Area, 3 Inter-Area, 5 AS External, 7 NSSA External. Type 0 means the information applies whatever the route type is.
  • AF: only 0, IPv4 unicast, is supported for now. The field exists to allow future extension.
  • Flags: the A-Flag (0x80, Attach) is set by an Area Border Router for an inter-area prefix that is locally connected or attached in another connected area. The N-Flag (0x40, Node) marks a host prefix that identifies the advertising router, typically a loopback address. It is ignored if the prefix is not a host prefix.
sections.eli5: The prefix note says which address block it is about, what kind of route it is, and gives a couple of yes/no flags. It can also carry extra stickers for any other details.

sections.title: The Extended Link Opaque LSA
sections.content:
The OSPFv2 Extended Link Opaque LSA uses Opaque Type 8 and always has LS Type 10, so its flooding scope is the area. It adds attributes for links advertised in Router-LSAs. Its TLV format is the same as in the prefix LSA.

The Extended Link TLV (type 1) describes exactly one link. It holds a Link Type, a Link ID and Link Data, with the first two meanings borrowed from the Router-LSA link definitions in RFC 2328, followed by sub-TLVs in any order. Only one Extended Link TLV SHALL appear in each Extended Link Opaque LSA, so a change to one link only needs a small update.

Neither TLV defines attributes by itself. The sub-TLV registries start with only a Reserved value of 0, so later specifications supply the attributes.
sections.eli5: The link note works the same way, but each note is about exactly one road, so changing one road does not mean rewriting a big note.

sections.title: Duplicates and Malformed LSAs
sections.content:
If the same prefix appears twice in one Extended Prefix LSA, only the first instance is used and the situation SHOULD be logged as an error. If it appears in different LSAs from the same router, the one with the smallest Opaque ID is used, which may be logged as a warning. Routers that repack TLVs between LSAs are RECOMMENDED to re-originate the LSAs in ascending Opaque ID order to minimize disruption. If different routers advertise the same prefix, the application using the data decides which LSA to prefer, for example the one with the best path to the prefix. The Extended Link TLV follows the same rules for links.

A malformed LSA is one whose TLV or sub-TLV overruns the end of its container, or where leftover data is smaller than a TLV header. Malformed LSAs MUST NOT be stored in the link state database, acknowledged or reflooded, and their receipt SHOULD be counted or logged.
sections.eli5: If two notes disagree, there are clear rules for which to believe. A note that is torn or cut off is thrown away and never passed on.

sections.title: Compatibility and Security
sections.content:
Opaque LSAs are optional and backward compatible, so these extensions are too. Future applications that use them MUST address backward compatibility of their own functionality.

The new LSAs face the same security concerns as those in RFC 2328 and the Opaque LSA specification. Applications must describe their own security considerations. Implementations must also make sure that malformed TLV and sub-TLV combinations cannot crash the router or its routing process.
sections.eli5: Old routers can ignore the new notes without breaking. Routers must also be careful not to trip over a badly written note.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content:
IANA registers Opaque Types 7 (Extended Prefix) and 8 (Extended Link) and creates five registries: the top-level TLVs for each LSA, the sub-TLVs for each TLV, and the Extended Prefix TLV Flags. The top-level registries start with 0 Reserved and 1 for the matching TLV. New values come from IETF Review or IESG Approval.

Types in the range 32768-33023 are for Experimental Use and MUST NOT be mentioned by RFCs, while 33024-65535 are not to be assigned until an IETF specification covers that range.
sections.eli5: There is an official list of note types, with a few numbers set aside for experiments and a few held back for later.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the value in octets, excluding padding.

fields.name: Route Type
fields.desc: Kind of OSPFv2 route; 0 means unspecified.

fields.name: Prefix Length
fields.desc: Length of the prefix in bits.

items.label: Unspecified
items.desc: Applies regardless of the prefix's route type.
